title: Topic 1.1 Introducing Statistics: What Can We Learn from Data?
text:
A question gives a study its direction
School A has 1,000 students enrolled this term. The school wants to understand how its students travel to school. Collecting information from every student would take time, so the investigator randomly selects 40 students and records their usual main travel methods.
The question concerns the whole school, whereas the recorded answers come from a selected group. Statistics connects those two levels: we use data from a sample to investigate a question about a population. The quality of that connection depends on how the study is designed, not just on doing arithmetic correctly.

section: Separate a group from its size
text:
Separate a group from its size








Component
Meaning
In the School A study




Population
All individuals or items the question is about
All students enrolled at School A this term


Population size, NN
Number of individuals or items in that population
N=1000N=1000 students


Sample
The selected individuals or items from which data are obtained
The 40 selected School A students


Sample size, nn
Number of individuals or items in that sample
n=40n=40 students



“The sample is 40” gives only its size. A complete identification is “the 40 selected students at School A.” Similarly, neither a percentage nor a mean is a group of people.
A population does not have to consist of people. It could consist of trees in a forest, books in a library, or products in a shipment. Name the group and its boundaries precisely enough that someone could decide whether a particular item belongs to it.

Explore: the sample is inside the population
Change the number selected and draw another illustrative selection. Notice what remains fixed.


Population: 1,000 hypothetical School A students. A selection of 40 students is a subset of that group, not a different population.


The interactive grid requires JavaScript; the explanation and practice below remain available without it.


The grid shows selection, not travel outcomes. Each mark represents one student; its position is simply a place in the grid, not a measured value. Selecting another sample changes who is observed. It does not change the population named in the investigative question.

title: Topic 1.1 Introducing Statistics: What Can We Learn from Data?
section: Why use a sample rather than a census?
text:
Why use a sample rather than a census?
A census attempts to collect the required information from every member of the population. A sample uses only part of the population. A census can be impractical when the population is large, access is difficult, collection is costly, or measurement uses up the item being tested.
For example, testing the breaking strength of every cable in a shipment would leave no unbroken cables to sell. A carefully planned sample can provide information while preserving the rest of the shipment.
Sample does not mean random sample. Random selection is a feature of the method, not part of the word “sample.” The School A example explicitly specifies random selection. We will study sampling methods and possible sources of bias later; a small or large nn alone does not tell us whether a study is trustworthy.

text:
Datum, data, and a data set
A datum is one piece of recorded information about an individual or item. Data is the plural; a data set is a collection of such information. Data can be category labels as well as numbers.
These illustrative records show how information can be organized:

“Student A mainly travels by bus” is one datum. “Student B has a 12.5-minute commute” is another. The table contains four students, not eight students: recording two characteristics for each student does not double the number of students.






TipCount individuals, not cells



If 40 students each answer three survey questions, the sample size is n=40n=40, not 120. The extra answers provide more information about those same students. Topic 1.2 develops the related terms observational unit and variable.

title: Topic 1.1 Introducing Statistics: What Can We Learn from Data?
section: Write an investigative question you can answer
text:
Write an investigative question you can answer
An investigative question states what the study is intended to find out. It should identify the relevant group and characteristic, and make it possible to decide what data to collect and analyze.







Wording
Assessment or improvement




“Are students’ journeys good?”
Too vague: which students, and what does “good” mean?


“What proportion of School A students enrolled this term mainly use the bus?”
A defined group and a specific characteristic; record each selected student’s main travel method.


“What is the mean one-way commute time for School A students this term?”
Answerable by recording comparable commute durations in a stated unit.


“Do you mainly use the bus?”
A question for one respondent. Its answers can supply data for the population-level investigative question.




Investigative question versus survey question
The investigative question belongs to the study. The survey question is asked of each respondent to obtain the information needed for that study. They serve different purposes and need not have identical wording.
For the bus-use study, asking “Which main travel method do you usually use?” is useful. Asking “What is your favourite subject?” would collect data, but those data would not answer the bus-use question.


Define how the information will be recorded
For this example, main travel method means the method used for the greatest distance on a typical school day. A student who walks to a stop and then takes a bus can now select one consistent answer. A real questionnaire would also specify how to handle a tie and provide an appropriate option for an unlisted method.
For commute time, specify a unit and common start/end points—for example, minutes from leaving home to reaching the school entrance. Otherwise, two students could interpret “commute time” differently.


Keep the original purpose intact
Set the investigative question before analyzing the results. Suppose a bus-use survey reveals interesting differences in satisfaction. Those differences may suggest a new follow-up study. They do not justify describing the original study as though its purpose had always been to investigate satisfaction.
This is not a ban on curiosity. It is a distinction between the question that motivated the study and a question suggested by what the investigator later noticed.

text:
Explain a result in context
In the fixed 40-response School A survey, 18 students report Bus as their main method. The sample calculation is
1840=0.45=45%.
\frac{18}{40}=0.45=45\%.

A clear statement is:

Among the 40 sampled School A students, 45% usually travel mainly by bus.

This sentence identifies the group, the characteristic, and the numerical result. It does not claim that exactly 45% of all 1,000 students use the bus. The sample result may inform the population question, but it is not automatically the exact population answer.
The fraction is included to practise contextual interpretation. The formal distinction between a parameter and a statistic, and symbols such as pp and p̂\hat p, is developed in Topic 1.2.

title: Topic 1.1 Introducing Statistics: What Can We Learn from Data?
text:
Practice: identify, formulate, justify
Attempt each question before expanding its solution. All questions below are original classroom practice.

1. Books in a library
A librarian wants to understand the binding condition of all 1,200 books in a library. She selects 60 books and records the condition of each binding.
Identify the population, sample, NN, and nn. Give one possible datum.

Solution. 


Show solution

The population is all 1,200 books in this library. The sample is the 60 selected books. Therefore N=1200N=1200 and n=60n=60.
One possible datum is “the binding of selected book 17 is loose.” The sample consists of books, not just books with loose bindings: condition is recorded after selection. The problem does not specify random selection, so do not add that claim.




2. Select information that answers the question
An investigator wants to estimate the proportion of the 800 students enrolled at School B this term who bring lunch from home on a typical school day. A random sample of 50 students is available.
Write an investigative question, one survey question, and a consistent recording rule.

Solution. 


Show solution

Investigative question: “What proportion of School B students enrolled this term usually bring lunch from home?”
Survey question: “During a usual five-day school week, on how many days do you bring lunch from home?” One possible rule is to classify three or more days as “usually,” with a stated convention for a nonstandard school week. Other well-defined rules are possible, but the same rule should apply to all respondents.
The population is all 800 enrolled students; the sample is the 50 selected students. Asking only whether they like the cafeteria would not answer the stated question.




3. Several measurements, one sample
A nursery selects 12 trees from its stock of 360 trees and records the height, trunk diameter, and species of each selected tree. A student says that the sample size is 36.
Explain the error and give the correct population and sample sizes.

Solution. 


Show solution

The sample contains 12 trees, so n=12n=12. The population contains all 360 trees in the nursery’s stock, so N=360N=360. There are 36 recorded characteristic values, but measuring three characteristics does not create three different trees.




4. Do not widen the population silently
A study asks about the travel methods of School A students enrolled this term. The investigator reports: “These results describe every teenager in the city.”
What is wrong with that conclusion? Repair it without claiming more than the study establishes.

Solution. 


Show solution

The city-wide group is broader than the stated population. Teenagers at other schools and teenagers not enrolled at School A are not included in the population defined by this study.
A safe description is “These data describe the travel responses of the sampled School A students this term.” With an appropriate design, the intended population-level target is the students enrolled at School A this term—not every teenager in the city.




5. Repair the report
A random sample of 80 households is selected from 2,400 households in a district; all 80 respond. Of the respondents, 52 report a working smoke alarm. The investigator writes: “The population is 80, and exactly 65% of all households have working alarms.”
Correct both problems. Show the sample calculation and write a contextual result.

Solution. 


Show solution

The population is all 2,400 households in the district, with N=2400N=2400. The sample is the 80 selected and responding households, with n=80n=80.
5280=0.65=65%.\frac{52}{80}=0.65=65\%.
Among the 80 sampled households, 65% reported a working smoke alarm. This is a sample result, not proof of the exact percentage among all 2,400 households. “Reported” also preserves what the survey actually measured; it does not claim an inspection was performed.




6. An unexpected finding
A survey was designed to study travel method. After noticing that many respondents dislike waiting at bus stops, an investigator rewrites the original purpose as “measuring dissatisfaction with bus stops.” Why is this misleading, and what could the investigator do instead?

Solution. 


Show solution

It represents a question suggested by the results as though it had been the purpose before the data were analyzed. Retain the original travel-method question in the report. Identify dissatisfaction as a later observation, then propose a separate, clearly described follow-up investigation with suitable questions and data collection.

title: Topic 1.2 Variables
text:
Observational unit, variable, and value
An observational unit is the individual or item on which information is recorded. A variable is a characteristic that can differ from one unit to another. A value is the particular outcome recorded for a variable on one unit.







Role
In the School A study




Observational unit
One selected School A student


Variable
That student’s usual main travel method


Possible values
Walk, Bicycle, Bus, Car, or another permitted method


One observed value
Bus for one particular student


A second variable
That student’s one-way commute time, in minutes



“Bus” is a value, not the name of the variable. “Students” names the units, not the characteristic being measured. A good variable description includes what is recorded and, for a measured quantity, its units.

Read a data table by rows and columns
The following four illustrative records repeat the examples from Topic 1.1. They illustrate table structure; they are not a raw-data extract of the fixed 40-response sample.



Student label
Main travel method
One-way commute time (minutes)




A
Bus
24.0


B
Walk
12.5


C
Car
18.0


D
Bus
31.5



Each row represents one student. The last two columns record two study variables on each student. The first column is an identifier, used to distinguish records. Recording two variables on four students still gives four observational units, not eight.
An identifier such as student number 1042 is a label, not a measured amount. Differences or averages of identifier numbers usually have no interpretation. Likewise, a characteristic is still a variable even when, by coincidence, every observed unit has the same recorded value.

title: Topic 1.2 Variables
text:
Categorical or quantitative?
A categorical (qualitative) variable records group membership or a label. A quantitative (numerical) variable records an amount obtained by counting or measuring.
Ask “What does a value represent?”, rather than “Does it contain digits?”








Variable recorded for each unit
Type
Reason




A student’s main travel method
Categorical
Bus and Walk identify categories.


A student’s one-way commute time
Quantitative
The value measures elapsed time, in minutes.


A student’s number of bus trips last week
Quantitative
The value counts trips; a difference of two means two more trips.


The route number of a bus used for one trip
Categorical
Route 10 and Route 20 identify routes; 20 does not mean twice as much travel.


A movie rating: Very dissatisfied through Very satisfied
Categorical, with an order
The labels express ordered levels, not measured distances between them.



Some categorical variables have a natural order. That order does not establish equal numerical gaps. Coding five satisfaction levels as 1–5, or relabelling them A–E, does not by itself turn satisfaction into a measured quantitative variable.

A frequency is not the original variable
For School A, main travel method is categorical. The frequency 18 is a numerical summary: it counts students whose recorded value is Bus. A numerical frequency table does not make the underlying travel-method variable quantitative.
The unit also matters. “Does this student use the bus?” gives a categorical Yes/No variable. “How many bus users attend this school?” gives a quantitative count, with a school as the observational unit.

title: Topic 1.2 Variables
text:
Discrete or continuous?
Classify a variable as categorical or quantitative first. Then, for a quantitative variable, ask which values are possible.
A discrete quantitative variable has a finite or countably infinite set of possible values. A continuous quantitative variable can, in its measurement model, take any value within an interval.








Variable
Classification
Explanation




Number of late arrivals during a five-day school week
Discrete
Possible counts are 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5. A count of 2.6 arrivals is not possible.


Number of pages in a book
Discrete
Pages are counted in whole numbers.


An examination score awarded only in half-point steps
Discrete
Values lie on a fixed grid: 0, 0.5, 1, 1.5, and so on. Discrete values need not be integers.


Actual elapsed time for a commute
Continuous
In principle, durations between 12 and 13 minutes are possible.


Actual mass of a parcel
Continuous
Mass is measured on a continuum, subject to measurement precision.




Rounding does not change the underlying quantity
A stopwatch may display a time of 12 minutes after rounding. The underlying elapsed time is still treated as continuous: it could have been 11.8 or 12.2 minutes. The rounded recorded values occur on a discrete grid, but the underlying variable being measured is continuous. State which one the question asks about.
Similarly, “has a decimal” does not prove continuous, and “is written as a whole number” does not prove discrete. Classification depends on the variable’s possible values and recording rule.

title: Topic 1.2 Variables
text:
Population summaries and sample summaries
A parameter is a numerical attribute or summary of a variable for the population. A statistic is a numerical attribute or summary of a variable for a sample.
The distinction is about which group the number describes, not how large the number is, whether it is known, or whether it is written as a percentage.








Quantity
Population parameter
Sample statistic




Proportion mainly travelling by bus
pp: proportion among all 1,000 School A students
p̂\hat p: proportion among the 40 sampled students


Mean one-way commute time
μ\mu: mean among all 1,000 School A students
x‾\bar x: mean among the 40 sampled students



Read p̂\hat p as “p-hat”, μ\mu as “mu”, and x‾\bar x as “x-bar.” These are common symbols, not substitutes for identifying the relevant group and variable. Recall that NN and nn denote population size and sample size, respectively; they are not the population and sample themselves.

Worked example: the sample bus proportion
Of the 40 sampled students, 18 report Bus. Therefore
p̂=1840=0.45=45%.\hat p=\frac{18}{40}=0.45=45\%.
This is a statistic, because it describes the 40 sampled School A students. The population parameter pp is the proportion of all 1,000 enrolled School A students who mainly travel by bus. Its value has not been supplied.
Do not write 18/100018/1000 for the sample proportion. The numerator counts bus riders in the sample, so the corresponding denominator is the sample size, 40. Do not assert that exactly 0.45(1000)=4500.45(1000)=450 students in the population use the bus: 450 would be an estimate based on the sample, not an observed population count.


Worked example: the sample mean
The fixed sample’s total commute time is 960 minutes, so
x‾=960 minutes40 students=24 minutes per student.\bar x=\frac{960\text{ minutes}}{40\text{ students}}=24\text{ minutes per student}.
The sample mean is 24 minutes, a statistic. The population mean μ\mu remains unknown. The fact that Student A in the illustrative table also has a 24-minute commute does not make that individual observation a sample mean; the two values play different roles.
A statistic can differ between samples. A population parameter refers to a fixed population and variable for the stated period, so drawing another sample does not change that target parameter.






TipKnown does not mean statistic



A census can reveal a population parameter. For example, if every one of the 80 parcels in a specified shipment is weighed, their mean mass is a parameter for that shipment, even though its numerical value is known. Identify the population before deciding.




Summary-role checkpoint
Distinguish a population summary, a sample summary, and a single observation. The group described by the number is the decisive evidence.


Without JavaScript: The School A sample’s 45% and 24-minute mean are statistics. The corresponding full-school summaries are parameters. One student’s recorded time is an individual datum, not a summary of the sample.

section: Relabelling categories does not create a measurement
text:
Relabelling categories does not create a measurement
Suppose we assign codes to the same four travel categories. The lab below leaves the 40 observations’ category memberships and counts unchanged, but changes the labels.


School A counts remain Walk 8, Bicycle 6, Bus 18, and Car 8. Codes 1, 2, 3, 4 give an arithmetic code average of 2.65; codes 4, 1, 9, 2 give 5.40. Neither average measures a travel method. The Bus proportion remains 18/40 = 45%.


Under codes Walk=1, Bicycle=2, Bus=3, Car=4, the arithmetic code average is
8(1)+6(2)+18(3)+8(4)40=2.65.\frac{8(1)+6(2)+18(3)+8(4)}{40}=2.65.
With Walk=4, Bicycle=1, Bus=9, Car=2, it becomes 5.40. Neither number means an “average travel method.” By contrast, the Bus proportion stays 45% under either one-to-one relabelling.
There is one useful special construction: define a numerical indicator equal to 1 for Bus and 0 otherwise. Its mean is 18/40=0.4518/40=0.45, the Bus proportion. This works because the coding explicitly counts membership in a chosen category. It does not justify taking the mean of arbitrary category codes, and combining all non-Bus categories loses their separate identities.

section: Data can also come from media
text:
Data can also come from media
A datum need not begin as a number in a spreadsheet. A photograph, audio clip, video, or written response can provide information about an observational unit. Define a characteristic and a consistent recording rule before classifying it.








Study material and observational unit
Recorded characteristic
Type




One photograph of a leaf
Leaf-edge category: smooth or toothed
Categorical


One recorded bird call
Actual call duration, in seconds
Continuous quantitative


One fixed-length traffic video clip
Number of bicycles passing a marked point
Discrete quantitative


One written survey response
Theme assigned using a stated coding rule
Categorical



The recording medium alone does not determine the variable type. A photograph could support either a category such as leaf shape or a measurement such as leaf length, provided an appropriate scale is available.

title: Topic 1.2 Variables
text:
Practice: identify and justify
These ten exercises are original classroom practice. Name the unit or group and give a reason, rather than only writing a classification label.

1. Rows, columns, and sample size
A researcher selects 12 library books and records each book’s catalogue number, binding type, number of pages, and mass in grams. Identify the observational unit, sample size, identifier, and the types of the other three variables.

Solution. 


Show full solution

The observational unit is one selected library book, and n=12n=12. Catalogue number is an identifier, not a measured amount. Binding type is categorical; page count is discrete quantitative; actual mass is continuous quantitative. Recording several characteristics does not increase the number of books sampled.




2. A number that is a label
For each bus trip, a student records route number 10, 20, or 25 and travel duration in minutes. Classify both variables and explain why the presence of digits is not sufficient.

Solution. 


Show full solution

The observational unit is one bus trip. Route number is categorical, because the number identifies a route; differences and ratios of route numbers do not measure travel. Actual duration is continuous quantitative, because it measures elapsed time. Digits can encode either a label or an amount.




3. Discrete does not mean “no decimals”
An assessment awards scores from 0 to 10 in half-point steps. A separate variable is the actual time needed to finish it. Classify both, even when the time is recorded to the nearest minute.

Solution. 


Show full solution

The score is discrete quantitative: its possible values are the 21 values 0,0.5,1,…,100,0.5,1,\ldots,10. The underlying elapsed time is continuous quantitative. Rounding restricts the displayed values, not the underlying duration. The classification would need to mention the discrete recording grid if the question specifically asked about the rounded recorded variable.




4. Same sample, two statistics
Use School A’s 40-student sample, its 18 Bus responses, and its total commute time of 960 minutes. Calculate and interpret p̂\hat p and x‾\bar x, then identify their population counterparts.

Solution. 


Show full solution

p̂=18/40=0.45\hat p=18/40=0.45: 45% of the sampled School A students mainly travel by bus. x‾=960/40=24\bar x=960/40=24 minutes: the sampled students’ mean one-way commute time is 24 minutes. Both are statistics. Their population counterparts are pp and μ\mu for all 1,000 enrolled School A students this term; neither population value is supplied.




5. Fix the denominator and the claim
A student writes, “There are 1,000 students at School A, so the bus proportion is 18/1000=1.8%18/1000=1.8\%.” Identify the problem and write a supported statement.

Solution. 


Show full solution

The 18 Bus responses were counted among the 40 sampled students, not all 1,000 students. The matching denominator is 40, giving 45%. A supported statement is: “Among the 40 sampled School A students, 45% mainly travel by bus.” The full population’s bus proportion is unknown from these summaries alone.




6. A known population parameter
A workshop has 80 finished parcels in a shipment. Every parcel is weighed, and the mean is 2.40 kg. In a separate quality check, 10 of those parcels have a mean of 2.31 kg. With the shipment as the population, classify both means.

Solution. 


Show full solution

The 2.40 kg mean describes all 80 parcels in the specified shipment, so it is a population parameter. The 2.31 kg mean describes only the 10 selected parcels, so it is a sample statistic. Being known does not change the parameter’s role, and the two means need not be equal.




7. Ordered categories and arbitrary codes
A movie survey uses Very dissatisfied, Dissatisfied, Neutral, Satisfied, and Very satisfied. Explain what is preserved when the labels are changed from 1–5 to A–E, and what is not justified by the numerical codes.

Solution. 


Show full solution

A one-to-one relabelling preserves category membership, frequencies, proportions, and the intended order, provided the code key is retained. It does not establish equal measured gaps between levels. The recorded satisfaction levels remain ordered categorical values; numerical coding alone does not justify interpreting their arithmetic mean as a measured amount of satisfaction.




8. Verify the recoding calculation
For Walk 8, Bicycle 6, Bus 18, and Car 8, use codes 4, 1, 9, and 2. Find the arithmetic average of these codes and the Bus proportion. Explain which result describes bus use meaningfully.

Solution. 


Show full solution

The code average is (8⋅4+6⋅1+18⋅9+8⋅2)/40=216/40=5.40(8\cdot4+6\cdot1+18\cdot9+8\cdot2)/40=216/40=5.40. It depends on arbitrary labels and has no travel-method interpretation. The Bus proportion is 18/40=0.45=45%18/40=0.45=45\%, which meaningfully describes the share of sampled students in the Bus category and is unchanged by the relabelling.




9. Change the observational unit
In Study I, each student’s record states whether they were late yesterday. In Study II, each school day’s record gives the number of late students. Identify the unit and variable type in each study.

Solution. 


Show full solution

In Study I, the unit is one student, and late yesterday (Yes/No) is categorical. In Study II, the unit is one school day, and the number of late students is discrete quantitative. Both concern lateness, but the units and recorded characteristics differ.




10. Extract two variables from a recording
A researcher makes 20 fixed-length traffic video clips at one intersection. For each clip, they record the weather category and the number of bicycles passing a marked line. Identify the observational unit, sample size, variable types, and one possible datum.

Solution. 


Show full solution

The unit is one video clip, and there are 20 clips, so the sample size is 20 for a study of those sampled clips. Weather category is categorical; number of passing bicycles is discrete quantitative. One possible datum is “Clip 7 shows 4 bicycles passing the marked line.” Neither the number of recorded characteristics nor the number of bicycles changes the count of observational units. A population-level claim would also require defining the target collection of clips or observation periods and considering how these clips were selected.

text:
One variable, one response per person
School A has 1,000 students enrolled this term. In our hypothetical sample of 40 School A students, each reports a usual main travel method: Walk, Bicycle, Bus, or Car. This is the same categorical study introduced in Topic 1.1; it is not the separate sample of 24 numerical commute times used in Topic 1.5.
The investigative question is: What proportion of School A students this term usually travel mainly by bus?
For a one-response frequency table, categories should be mutually exclusive (a respondent cannot be counted in two categories) and collectively exhaustive (every valid response has a place). Here, main method means the method used for the greatest distance on a typical school day. A real questionnaire should also provide consistent rules for ties or unlisted methods; our hypothetical data specify exactly one method for each of the 40 respondents.

section: Ratios change when the denominator changes
text:
Ratios change when the denominator changes
A part-to-whole ratio compares one category to the entire group. The ratio Bus to all responses is 18:40=9:2018:40=9:20, which represents the same share as 18/40=45%18/40=45\%.
A part-to-part ratio compares two categories. Bus to Car is 18:8=9:418:8=9:4, and 18/8=2.2518/8=2.25 means that there are 2.25 times as many sampled bus riders as sampled car riders. It does not mean that 225% of all sampled students take the bus.

Activity: the denominator explorer
Select the numerator category and the group being used as the denominator. Explain who is included in the denominator before examining the result.


Static reference: Bus among all 40 respondents is 18/40=45%18/40=45\%. Bus compared with Car is 18:8=9:418:8=9:4.


For another comparison, Bus among only Bus-or-Bicycle respondents is 18/(18+6)=18/24=75%18/(18+6)=18/24=75\%. The category count did not change; the group described did. Ratios become interpretable only when both sides are labelled.

section: Most common is not always a majority
text:
Most common is not always a majority
A modal category is the category with the greatest frequency. Bus is the most common category because 18 exceeds the counts 8, 6, and 8. This is a plurality, not a majority: 18/40=45%18/40=45\% is below 50%.
Because Walk and Bicycle are disjoint categories, they can be combined: 8+6=148+6=14 students, or 14/40=35%14/40=35\%, reported Walk or Bicycle. Do not add counts that overlap. In a choose every method used survey, a respondent may check both Walk and Bus and the total category selections can exceed the number of respondents.
A supported statement is: “Among the 40 sampled School A students, Bus was the most common usual main travel method, reported by 18 students (45%).” An unsupported overstatement is “Exactly 45% of all 1,000 School A students travel by bus.” The sample does not reveal the exact population proportion.

Checkpoint: what does the table justify?
The four original cases begin with no answer selected. Choose, check the explanation, clear your choice, or move to the next case.


Static reference: Bus is the largest category (45%) but not a majority; Walk or Bicycle accounts for 35% of this sample.

3. The majority mistake
A student writes, “Bus is the largest category, so the majority of respondents take the bus.” Identify exactly what is right and wrong.

Solution. 


Show solution

Bus is the largest individual category: 18 exceeds 8, 6, and 8. But a majority is more than half; 18/40=45%<50%18/40=45\%<50\%. Correct report: “Bus was the most common main method among the 40 sampled students, reported by 18 (45%), but fewer than half chose it.”




4. Two different denominators
Compute (a) Bus to Bicycle as a simplified ratio, (b) Bus among all 40 responses, and (c) Bus among Bus-or-Bicycle responses.

Solution. 


Show solution


18:6=3:118:6=3:1; (b) 18/40=0.45=45%18/40=0.45=45\%; (c) 18/(18+6)=18/24=0.75=75%18/(18+6)=18/24=0.75=75\%. The numerator is unchanged, while the denominator for (c) includes only the 24 sampled people in the selected pair of categories.





5. Why don’t the counts sum to 30?
A check every method used survey has 30 respondents and counts Walk 18, Bus 12, Bicycle 8, Car 7, totalling 45. Is the table necessarily wrong? Must percentages of respondents selecting each method add to 100%?

Solution. 


Show solution

No. Respondents may select more than one method; the 45 selections can come from 30 people. Dividing by 30 gives 60%, 40%, 26.7%, 23.3% of respondents selecting each method, summing to approximately 150%. These are overlapping categories, not a single-answer distribution whose relative frequencies must sum to 100%.




6. A misleading denominator
A report says, “Bus accounts for 18% of School A’s 1,000 students because 18 sampled students chose Bus.” Correct the calculation and statement.

Solution. 


Show solution

The appropriate denominator for the sampled bus count is 40 sampled students. The sample percentage is 18/40=45%18/40=45\%, not 18%. A defensible report is “Among 40 sampled School A students, 18 (45%) reported Bus as their usual main method.” The exact percentage among all 1,000 students is not known from these data.




7. Rounding is not missing data
Three categories each contain one person in a survey of three. The reported percentages, 33.3%, 33.3%, and 33.3%, sum to 99.9%. Has one person been left out?

Solution. 


Show solution

No. 1+1+1=31+1+1=3 includes everyone. The exact proportions are 1/31/3 each and sum to 1. Rounding each 100/3%100/3\% to one decimal creates the 0.1-percentage-point difference.

text:
1 · Bar charts: compare category heights
A frequency bar chart uses one separate bar per category; bar height (or length) gives the count. Draw four bars of equal width with heights 8, 6, 18, 8. Label the vertical axis Number of sampled students, the horizontal axis Usual main travel method, and begin the vertical scale at zero.
A relative-frequency bar chart uses the same categories but bar heights 20%, 15%, 45%, 20%. Its vertical axis should say Percent of sampled students. The gap between bars emphasizes that categories are separate: bar charts are not histograms, which group numerical values into intervals (see Topic 1.5).
Design rule: A truncated vertical axis can exaggerate relative bar lengths. For instance, a bar at 18 and one at 8 should be visibly 18 and 8 units long from the common zero baseline. A chart with an unexplained lower cutoff may mislead readers.






TipCount versus percentage



Counts answer how many; percentages answer what share of the relevant group. Include sample size and units. A most-common (modal) category is not necessarily a majority: School A’s Bus group contains 18/40 = 45%, which is less than 50%.

text:
4 · Write a supported statement
A complete interpretation says which students, which variable/category, which measure, and what values support the claim.
Supported: “Among the 40 sampled School A students, Bus was the most common usual main travel method, reported by 18 students (45%).”
Unsupported: “A majority of all School A students take the bus.” Forty-five percent of the sample is not a majority, and the population percentage is unknown.
Supported comparison: “Bus made up a greater proportion of the School A sample (45%) than of the School B sample (30%).” That describes samples, not an established difference between populations.

Preserve the meaning of ordered categories
For a separate hypothetical movie-satisfaction survey, the ordered categories Very dissatisfied, Dissatisfied, Neutral, Satisfied, Very satisfied have counts 2, 4, 5, 12, 7 (total 30). Keep the bar-chart categories in their natural order. One-to-one recoding as 1–5 or A–E retains category identity and order, but does not establish equal numerical spacing between levels. Merging adjacent categories loses information. It remains an ordered categorical variable, even when its labels are numerals.

title: Topic 1.4 Graphical Representations for One Categorical Variable
text:
Practice: construct, compare, explain
All eight problems and solutions below are original classroom exercises. Try each before opening the worked answer.

1. Build two School A bar charts
Specify the heights, labels, and baseline for both the count and relative-frequency bar charts.

Solution. 


Show worked solution

Use category order Walk, Bicycle, Bus, Car. Count heights: 8, 6, 18, 8 with vertical axis “Number of sampled students.” Percentage heights: 20%, 15%, 45%, 20% with vertical axis “Percent of 40 sampled School A students.” Both axes start at zero. Use equal-width separated bars and label the horizontal axis “Usual main travel method.”




2. Calculate every School A pie angle
Show the four calculations and check that the slices form a circle.

Solution. 


Show worked solution

Walk: (8/40)360∘=72∘(8/40)360^\circ=72^\circ. Bicycle: (6/40)360∘=54∘(6/40)360^\circ=54^\circ. Bus: (18/40)360∘=162∘(18/40)360^\circ=162^\circ. Car: (8/40)360∘=72∘(8/40)360^\circ=72^\circ. Check: 72+54+162+72=360 degrees; the four sample proportions sum to 100%.




3. Calculate School B pie angles
Find every percentage and slice angle from 9, 6, 18, and 27 responses out of 60.

Solution. 


Show worked solution

Walk: 9/60=15%9/60=15\%, angle 54°. Bicycle: 6/60=10%6/60=10\%, angle 36°. Bus: 18/60=30%18/60=30\%, angle 108°. Car: 27/60=45%27/60=45\%, angle 162°. The percentages total 100% and angles total 360°. Use 60 as the denominator throughout.




4. Equal counts imply equal shares?
Someone writes, “School A and School B each have 18 sampled bus riders, so bus use is equally common in their samples.” Evaluate.

Solution. 


Show worked solution

The counts are both 18, but the sample proportions are 18/40=45% and 18/60=30%. The School A sample’s bus share is 15 percentage points greater. Equal counts with different denominators do not imply equal shares.




5. Compare sampled car users
How much greater is School B’s sample Car share than School A’s, in percentage points?

Solution. 


Show worked solution

School A: 8/40=20%8/40=20\%. School B: 27/60=45%27/60=45\%. The difference is 45%-20%=25 percentage points. The data do not establish the exact difference between the full populations.




6. Audit a truncated scale
A bar graph comparing counts Bus=18 and Car=8 begins its vertical axis at 7. What is wrong with that display?

Solution. 


Show worked solution

Bars encode magnitude through length from a baseline. Omitting 0–7 makes the visible lengths 11 and 1 units, visually exaggerating the difference. A conventional count bar chart should start its y-axis at 0, with bars of heights 18 and 8 and a labelled scale.




7. Order the movie ratings
Why should Very dissatisfied → Very satisfied remain in order after one-to-one recoding as A–E? Does A–E make the variable quantitative?

Solution. 


Show worked solution

The five levels have a meaningful order, so preserving it lets viewers see the satisfaction pattern from low to high. Recoding levels as A, B, C, D, E changes labels, not counts or category meaning; it does not make the variable quantitative or imply equal distances between levels.




8. Study-location pie or bar?
A separate hypothetical sample of 24 students reports Home 9, Library 8, Cafe 4, Other 3. Find Home’s pie angle. Is Home a majority? Which graph better distinguishes Home from Library?

Solution. 


Show worked solution

Home: 9/24=37.5%9/24=37.5\% and (9/24)360∘=135∘(9/24)360^\circ=135^\circ. It is the modal category, but not a majority because 37.5% is less than 50%. A labelled bar chart more clearly distinguishes the close frequencies 9 versus 8 than a pie chart’s similar slice angles.

title: Topic 1.5 Graphical Representations for One Quantitative Variable
text:
Learning goal: Construct and interpret dotplots and stem-and-leaf plots while preserving numerical order, units, and repeated values.


Start with the variable
An observational unit is one student. The variable is that student’s one-way commute time, in minutes. A distribution tells us which values occur and how often they occur.
For quantitative data, position measures an amount. The distance from 10 to 20 minutes must represent the same change as the distance from 20 to 30 minutes. We cannot reorder the numbers as we sometimes reorder unordered category labels.
Our sorted data are:
5, 8, 10, 12, 12, 14, 15, 16, 18, 18, 20, 20,
22, 24, 25, 26, 28, 30, 32, 35, 38, 42, 48, 58
Download the 24 recorded values as CSV.


A dotplot: one dot for every observation
Draw a labelled numerical axis. Place one dot at each recorded value. When a value repeats, stack the dots vertically. Two dots at 12 mean two students, each with a 12-minute commute—not one student with a 24-minute commute.


There are 24 dots; the recorded values 12, 18, and 20 each occur twice.


The axis extends from 0 to 60, but the observations extend from 5 to 58. Axis endpoints are not automatically observed values. A dotplot preserves recorded values, but not the original order of data collection.


A stem and a leaf reconstruct one value
For these whole-minute times, use tens digits as stems and ones digits as leaves:
28=10(2)+8,key: 2∣8=28 minutes.28=10(2)+8,\qquad \text{key: }2\mid8=28\text{ minutes}.
Write stems in increasing order. Sort the leaves within each row. Keep repeated leaves and zeros: each leaf still represents one observation. Include intermediate empty stems when necessary so a gap is not hidden.
Stem | Leaves
  0  | 5 8
  1  | 0 2 2 4 5 6 8 8
  2  | 0 0 2 4 5 6 8
  3  | 0 2 5 8
  4  | 2 8
  5  | 8
Key: 2 | 8 = 28 minutes
Read the key first. With the key 1∣2=1.21\mid2=1.2 seconds, the same printed digits would represent different measurements. A stem may contain more than one digit; a leaf is usually one digit.


Replay the construction
Choose a display, then add observations. The activity uses our 24 times in a mixed order so you can see repeated values finding their proper positions.


Use JavaScript to add the 24 values one at a time. The completed plots are also shown above.




Check your understanding
How many students recorded at least 40 minutes? Which exact values did they record?


Show solution

There are three students, with recorded times 42, 48, and 58 minutes. Both displays preserve individual values, so the conclusion is exact at the precision of the recorded data.







TipBefore you move on



Recover a sorted list by writing one entry for every dot or leaf. Counting only unique positions would lose repeated observations.

title: Topic 1.5 Graphical Representations for One Quantitative Variable
text:
Build a histogram

Learning goal: Choose and read bins, tally observations, and draw one complete bar for each row of the frequency table.


Step 1 · Choose and read the bins
A histogram groups quantitative observations into ordered intervals called bins. A bar’s width represents an interval of the variable; its height gives the frequency or relative frequency in that interval. We use equal-width bins throughout this lesson.
The commute times run from 5 to 58 minutes. A display spanning 0–60 minutes with width 10 covers every observation:


Boundaries: 0, 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60 minutes; six bins of width 10.


number of bins=60−010=6.\text{number of bins}=\frac{60-0}{10}=6.
Seven boundary marks produce six intervals, not seven bins. For a span SS, equal bin width ww, and number of bins kk, S=kwS=kw when the bins exactly partition the span.

Use one consistent endpoint rule
Our convention is left-inclusive and right-exclusive:
a≤x<b.a\leq x<b.
Thus 20 enters 20≤x<3020\leq x<30, not 10≤x<2010\leq x<20. Every observation must enter exactly one bin. Other conventions are possible but must be clearly stated. Here, 58 is below 60 and enters the final bin. A value equal to the final right boundary would require an explicit endpoint exception or an additional bin.

Step 3 · Draw one whole bar per table row
Start the frequency axis at zero and use an even scale. The first row has frequency 2, so draw the first bar to height 2. The next row has frequency 8, so draw the entire next bar to height 8. Adjacent bins share boundaries; their bars touch. An empty bin has zero height.


The six table rows produce whole bars with heights 2, 8, 7, 4, 2, and 1.


The 10-to-under-20-minute bar represents eight students, not an 8-minute commute. Frequency is on one axis; the commute-time interval is on the other. A horizontal histogram reverses the axes: intervals are vertical and frequencies are horizontal.


Frequency or relative frequency?
For a bin with frequency ff in a sample of size nn,
relative frequency=fn,percentage=fn×100%.\text{relative frequency}=\frac{f}{n},\qquad
\text{percentage}=\frac{f}{n}\times100\%.
The second bin has 8/24=1/3≈33.3%8/24=1/3\approx33.3\% of the observations. Every bin uses the same denominator, 24. Scaling all bars by the same factor changes the numerical axis, not their relative pattern.


Frequency counts: 2, 8, 7, 4, 2, 1. Their relative frequencies use denominator 24.




A histogram is not a categorical bar chart
These examples use different illustrative samples: travel method for 40 students, and commute time for 24 students.

NoteWhat is no longer visible?



Height 7 for 20≤x<3020\leq x<30 does not reveal the seven exact times. A histogram usually cannot reconstruct the original observations. Use a dotplot, stem-and-leaf plot, or raw list when exact values matter.

text:
Histogram laboratory

Learning goal: Explain why different histograms can represent exactly the same data.


Change the bins, not the observations
This lab always uses the same 24 commute times. The numerical span remains 0–60 minutes. Choose either a bin width or a number of equal-width bins. Switch the vertical axis between counts and percentages.
Click a bar—or focus it and press Enter—to inspect its interval and recorded values. The width and bin-count controls are alternative ways to specify the same partition.


At width 10 minutes there are six bins with frequencies 2, 8, 7, 4, 2, 1. JavaScript enables the adjustable version.








NoteA fair visual comparison



The frequency scale remains 0–24, or the percentage scale 0–100%. Changing bins does not quietly rescale the vertical axis. Some bars may look short; every graph still represents all 24 students.




Investigate before revealing
1. Compare widths of 5, 10, and 20 minutes. Which view shows more local detail? Which could conceal gaps or separate concentrations?


Show explanation

Width 5 gives 12 bins; width 10 gives 6; width 20 gives 3. Narrow bins show more local detail but can look irregular. Wide bins smooth over detail and may hide gaps or multiple concentrations. No single appearance tells the whole story.

2. With width 10, inspect the third bin. Does height 7 mean seven students recorded exactly 20 minutes?


Show explanation

No. The interval contains 20, 20, 22, 24, 25, 26, and 28 minutes. Only two values equal 20. The panel’s exact values come from the underlying data supplied to the lab—not from the bar itself.

3. Change the number of bins to 9. What changes, and what stays fixed?


Show explanation

The width becomes 60/9≈6.66760/9\approx6.667 minutes. Boundaries, counts per bin, and appearance change. The 24 recorded values, minimum 5, and maximum 58 do not. Boundary labels may be rounded; assignment uses unrounded boundaries.



A gap can disappear from the histogram
This separate clinic dataset has concentrations near 5–12 and 24–30 minutes and one unusually long wait of 55 minutes.


No clinic times lie strictly between 12 and 24 minutes, or between 30 and 55 minutes.




Twenty-minute bins give counts 10, 9, and 1. All bins are nonempty despite the gaps in the raw data.


A zero-frequency bin establishes that its entire interval contains no observations. The reverse does not hold: nonempty bins may contain smaller empty regions. Coarse bins can hide gaps visible in individual-value displays.

title: Topic 1.6 Descriptions for One Quantitative Variable Distributions
text:
Learning goal: Describe shape, approximate center, spread, and unusual features in context, then support your description with graph evidence.


The four-part description








Part
Ask yourself
Include in the response




Shape
Symmetry or skew? How many main peaks?
Overall balance and prominent peaks


Center
Where is a central value?
A numerical location, with units


Spread
How widely do values vary?
An interval or overall span, with units


Unusual features
Gaps, clusters, or potential outliers?
Approximate locations and evidence



Always name the variable, group, and units. Write “commute times among these 24 students,” not just “the graph.” A description is more than a list of vocabulary words.


Skew is named for the longer tail
Right-skewed distributions have a longer tail toward larger values. Left-skewed distributions have a longer tail toward smaller values. Approximately symmetric means the sides roughly mirror each other. The tallest bars do not identify the direction of skew.


Right-skewed illustration: many smaller values, with a tail toward larger values.




Left-skewed illustration: many larger values, with a tail toward smaller values.




Peaks answer a different question
Unimodal means one main peak; bimodal means two prominent peaks. Approximately uniform means similar frequencies across equal-width intervals, without prominent peaks. Two adjacent tall bars may form one broad peak; not every small bump is a separate mode.


Hypothetical illustrations: symmetric with one broad peak; symmetric and bimodal; approximately uniform.


A distribution may be symmetric and bimodal. Symmetric does not necessarily mean bell-shaped. These are teaching illustrations; the next activity uses published observations.


Shape detective: published data
Inspect each histogram before choosing A–E. These are the published datasets from the revised lecture, not repeated versions of the schematic examples. Approximate descriptions allow ordinary irregularities in real data.


Cases: major North American river lengths, Old Faithful waiting times, and Iris setosa sepal lengths. Source links appear with each case.




Center and spread are different
The next hypothetical group has 30 practice-task times. Its balance is easy to see near 20 minutes. Observations extend from 12 to 28 minutes, giving an overall span of 28−12=1628-12=16 minutes.


Symmetric task-time data centered at 20 minutes; minimum 12, maximum 28.


“About 20 minutes is central” answers a different question from “values span 16 minutes.” Do not use the height of the tallest bar as the center: that height is a count, not a value of the variable.


Clusters, gaps, and potential outliers
Clusters are concentrations of observations. A gap is an interval between observed values containing no observations. An outlier is unusually small or large relative to the rest; a graph may identify a potential outlier for investigation.


Clinic times cluster at 5–12 and 24–30 minutes, with an isolated value at 55 minutes.


Here, 55 minutes is unusually separated from the main groups. It is not automatically a recording error and should not automatically be deleted. A single high-end observation does not, by itself, require the outlier label.






TipA useful sentence frame



“Among [group], the distribution of [variable and units] is [shape], centered around [value or interval], and extends from about [lower end] to [upper end]. [Describe any notable gap, cluster, or unusual value.]”
Use approximate language for graphical estimates. With two separated concentrations, explain both instead of treating a central value in the gap as a typical observation.

text:
Worked examples and evidence

Describe the commute histogram
Use only this grouped display. Remembering the raw list is different from reading evidence from a histogram.


Six 10-minute bins starting at zero have frequencies 2, 8, 7, 4, 2, 1.


The shape is roughly unimodal and right-skewed. The center is approximately in the 20–30 minute interval. Occupied bins extend from 0–10 through 50–60 minutes. There is no empty 10-minute bin and just one observation in the last bin.

Among these 24 students, recorded commute times are roughly unimodal and right-skewed, centered in the 20–30 minute interval. Values occupy bins from 0 to under 10 through 50 to under 60 minutes. No displayed bin is empty, although smaller gaps may be hidden inside bins.

Do not report an exact minimum of 5 or maximum of 58 from this graph alone. Those facts require the individual observations.


Support a claim numerically
Claim: Most of these students recorded commute times under 30 minutes.
2+8+7=17 students,1724×100%≈70.8%.2+8+7=17\text{ students},\qquad \frac{17}{24}\times100\%\approx70.8\%.
Seventeen is more than half of 24, so the claim is supported. Write: “About 71% of these sampled students recorded a commute time under 30 minutes.” Do not silently extend the conclusion to every student at the school.


Evidence check
Decide what the histogram alone establishes. Each new statement begins with no answer selected.


Four statements test bin counts, exact values, majority, and the exact maximum.



A threshold inside a bin
Exactly 2+1=32+1=3 times are at least 40 minutes. But at least 45 minutes splits the 40–50 bin. Its two observations could lie below or above 45; the one in 50–60 definitely qualifies. Therefore between 1 and 3 students could qualify from the histogram alone. Do not assume uniformity inside a bin.



Dissolved oxygen in cold streams
The revised lecture uses 2023 AP Statistics Free-Response Question 1(a). The official question, PDF page 4 contains the original figure. Below is a classroom redraw from the printed frequencies, not an official College Board graphic.
The variable is dissolved oxygen concentration, in mg/L, for sampled Alaskan streams colder than 8°C.


One-unit bins from 2 to 14 mg/L have frequencies 1, 0, 1, 1, 13, 12, 15, 40, 94, 117, 89, 46; total 429.









Feature
Evidence




Shape
One peak at 11–12 mg/L; tail toward smaller values


Center
About 11–12 mg/L


Spread
Occupied bins extend across roughly 2–14 mg/L


Unusual features
Empty 3–4 bin; potentially unusual low values below 6 mg/L





Show the complete model response

For these sampled Alaskan streams colder than 8°C, dissolved oxygen concentrations are unimodal and left-skewed, centered around 11–12 mg/L. Occupied bins extend across roughly 2–14 mg/L, with a gap in the 3–4 mg/L bin and several potentially unusual low measurements below 6 mg/L. The boundaries do not reveal the exact minimum and maximum.


Follow-up calculation
The total frequency is 429. The four bins from 10 to under 14 mg/L contain
94+117+89+46=346,346429×100%≈80.7%.94+117+89+46=346,\qquad \frac{346}{429}\times100\%\approx80.7\%.
About 81% of these sampled cold streams occupy those bins. Height 117 means 117 observations in the whole 11–12 mg/L interval, not exactly 11. These classroom follow-ups use our left-inclusive, right-exclusive convention; they are not additional parts of the original exam.



Recover values from a dotplot
The lecture identifies these numerical data as transcribed from the 2022 AP Statistics Question 5 chocolate dotplots. The book shows a new classroom rendering of that transcription; it does not upload the exam screenshot. Original-material availability is managed by College Board’s exam archive.


Two dotplots show recorded reductions in blood pressure in mmHg.


Read one entry per dot, including stacked dots. What are the two sorted lists?


Show the recovered lists

Dark Chocolate (13 observations):
-3, -1, 0, 2, 4, 5, 7, 8, 9, 10, 10, 12, 16
White Chocolate (12 observations):
-12, -6, -3, -3, -2, -2, 2, 3, 4, 4, 5, 15
Units are mmHg of reduction. Negative reduction means blood pressure increased; zero means no change. The order is sorted, not the original observation order. Our task here is data recovery, not a causal conclusion about the treatments.

4 · Repair turnaround times
Describe the histogram of 40 bicycle repairs. Find the percentage taking at least 4 hours. Can you recover the most common exact time?


One-hour bins from 0 to 8: frequencies 12, 10, 7, 5, 3, 2, 1, 0.




Show solution

Repair times are unimodal and right-skewed, centered around 1–3 hours. Values occupy bins from 0 to under 7 hours. No displayed internal bin is empty. The one observation in 6–7 hours is not automatically an outlier; an empty final 7–8 bin is not an internal gap.
At least 4 hours: (3+2+1)/40=15%(3+2+1)/40=15\%. The most frequent interval is 0–1 hour. The most common exact value is not recoverable.

5 · Two concentrations
Describe shape, center, spread, and the empty internal interval for these 40 library study sessions. What percentage lasted from 30 to under 90 minutes?


Fifteen-minute bins from 0 to 120: frequencies 2, 10, 8, 0, 0, 8, 10, 2.




Show solution

The displayed distribution is approximately symmetric and bimodal, with main concentrations in 15–45 and 75–105 minutes. The visual center near 60 minutes lies in a gap, not at a typical observed session. Occupied bins span roughly 0–120 minutes. There are no observations from 45 to under 75 minutes.
The count from 30 to under 90 is 8+0+0+8=168+0+0+8=16, giving 16/40=40%16/40=40\%. A single center would hide the two concentrations. The exact median is not available from the histogram.

Two commute times lie in 40–50 and one in 50–60 minutes. How many are at least 40? How many could be at least 45?
